questions.explanation_text: In an ether, the larger carbon part is chosen as the parent hydrocarbon, and the smaller part attached through oxygen is named as an alkoxy group. Here, one side of oxygen is an ethyl group, $-C_{2}H_{5}$ . So this part becomes the alkoxy group: ethoxy, $-O-C_{2}H_{5}$ . The other side is a tert-butyl group, $-C(CH_{3})_{3}$ . The longest continuous chain in this part has 3 carbon atoms, so the parent hydrocarbon is propane. In the propane chain, the middle carbon is carbon number 2. Both substituents are attached to this carbon. At carbon 2, there is one methyl group, $-CH_{3}$ , and one ethoxy group, $-O-C_{2}H_{5}$ . Substituents are written in alphabetical order. Ethoxy comes before methyl. So, the correct IUPAC name is 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane .
questions.explanation_html:
In an ether, the larger carbon part is chosen as the parent hydrocarbon, and the smaller part attached through oxygen is named as an alkoxy group.

Here, one side of oxygen is an ethyl group, $-C_{2}H_{5}$ . So this part becomes the alkoxy group: ethoxy, $-O-C_{2}H_{5}$ .

The other side is a tert-butyl group, $-C(CH_{3})_{3}$ . The longest continuous chain in this part has 3 carbon atoms, so the parent hydrocarbon is propane.

In the propane chain, the middle carbon is carbon number 2. Both substituents are attached to this carbon.

At carbon 2, there is one methyl group, $-CH_{3}$ , and one ethoxy group, $-O-C_{2}H_{5}$ .

Substituents are written in alphabetical order. Ethoxy comes before methyl.

So, the correct IUPAC name is 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane.

questions.explanation_text: Glycerol is a trihydric alcohol, so it contains three alcoholic groups. Its structure is: $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}-\text{CHOH}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ Now look at the carbon atoms attached to the $-OH$ groups. The two end carbon atoms are $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ groups. Each of these carbon atoms is attached to only one other carbon atom, so these are primary alcoholic groups. The middle carbon atom is $\text{CHOH}$ . It is attached to two other carbon atoms, so this is a secondary alcoholic group. So glycerol contains: $\text{two primary and one secondary alcoholic groups}$ Correct option: B. Two primary and one secondary alcoholic groups.
questions.explanation_html:
Glycerol is a trihydric alcohol, so it contains three alcoholic groups.

Its structure is:

$\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}-\text{CHOH}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$

Now look at the carbon atoms attached to the $-OH$ groups.

The two end carbon atoms are $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ groups. Each of these carbon atoms is attached to only one other carbon atom, so these are primary alcoholic groups.

The middle carbon atom is $\text{CHOH}$ . It is attached to two other carbon atoms, so this is a secondary alcoholic group.

So glycerol contains:

$\text{two primary and one secondary alcoholic groups}$

Correct option: B. Two primary and one secondary alcoholic groups.

questions.explanation_text: $R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ is a primary alcohol. To convert a primary alcohol into an aldehyde, we need a mild oxidising agent. PCC oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes without further oxidising them to carboxylic acids. $R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}\overset{\text{PCC}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}R-\text{CHO}$ Alkaline $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ is a strong oxidising agent, so it usually oxidises primary alcohols further to carboxylic acids: $R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}\overset{\text{alkaline}KMnO_{4}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}R-\text{COOH}$ $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ and $\text{Na}/\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ are reducing agents, so they are not used for this oxidation. So the correct answer is: $\text{Option D: PCC (Pyridinium Chlorochromate)}$
questions.explanation_html:
$R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ is a primary alcohol.

To convert a primary alcohol into an aldehyde, we need a mild oxidising agent. PCC oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes without further oxidising them to carboxylic acids.

$R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}\overset{\text{PCC}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}R-\text{CHO}$

Alkaline $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ is a strong oxidising agent, so it usually oxidises primary alcohols further to carboxylic acids:

$R-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}\overset{\text{alkaline}KMnO_{4}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}R-\text{COOH}$

$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ and $\text{Na}/\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ are reducing agents, so they are not used for this oxidation.

So the correct answer is:

$\text{Option D: PCC (Pyridinium Chlorochromate)}$

questions.question_html:
$\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\overset{(i)\text{BH}_{3};(ii)\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}/\text{NaOH}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}P\overset{\text{CrO}_{3},\text{anhydrous medium}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}Q\overset{(i)\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr};(ii)\text{H}_{2}\text{O}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}R+\text{Mg(OH)Br}$
The organic compounds $P,Q$ and $R$ are

options.label: A
B
C

questions.explanation_text: The starting material $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}$ is propene, $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$ . When propene reacts with $\text{BH}_{3}$ and then with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}/\text{NaOH}$ , hydroboration-oxidation takes place. In this reaction, water adds across the double bond in the anti-Markovnikov way. So the $-\text{OH}$ group goes to the terminal carbon. So propene changes into 1-propanol. $P=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{OH}$ Now $P$ is a primary alcohol. When a primary alcohol is oxidised using $\text{CrO}_{3}$ in an anhydrous medium, it forms an aldehyde and does not go further to a carboxylic acid. So 1-propanol changes into propanal. $Q=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CHO}$ Now propanal reacts with the Grignard reagent $\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr}$ . The $\text{CH}_{3}$ group gets added to the carbonyl carbon of propanal. After hydrolysis with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ , a secondary alcohol is formed. $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CHO}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr}\overset{\text{H}_{2}\text{O}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_{3}+\text{Mg(OH)Br}$ So $R$ is 2-butanol. $R=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
The starting material $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}$ is propene, $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$ .

When propene reacts with $\text{BH}_{3}$ and then with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}/\text{NaOH}$ , hydroboration-oxidation takes place. In this reaction, water adds across the double bond in the anti-Markovnikov way. So the $-\text{OH}$ group goes to the terminal carbon.

So propene changes into 1-propanol.

$P=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{OH}$

Now $P$ is a primary alcohol. When a primary alcohol is oxidised using $\text{CrO}_{3}$ in an anhydrous medium, it forms an aldehyde and does not go further to a carboxylic acid.

So 1-propanol changes into propanal.

$Q=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CHO}$

Now propanal reacts with the Grignard reagent $\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr}$ . The $\text{CH}_{3}$ group gets added to the carbonyl carbon of propanal. After hydrolysis with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ , a secondary alcohol is formed.

$\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CHO}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr}\overset{\text{H}_{2}\text{O}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_{3}+\text{Mg(OH)Br}$

So $R$ is 2-butanol.

$R=\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_{3}$

questions.explanation_text: The reactions of ethanol with metals (e.g., sodium) indicate its acidic nature. It reacts with active metals such as sodium to yield corresponding alkoxide and hydrogen $2R-OH+2Na \rightarrow \underset{Sodiumalkoxide}{2R-\bar{O}-\overset{+}{N}a}+H_{2}$ The acidic character of alcohols is due to the polar nature of $O-H$ bond. These are weaker acids than water.

questions.explanation_text: Key Idea Acidic strength is inversely proportional to the $pK_{a}$ value. The correct match is $a \rightarrow iii,b \rightarrow iv,c \rightarrow i,d \rightarrow ii$ Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. The ionisation of an alcohol and a phenol takes place as follows In alkoxide ion, the negative charge is localised on oxygen while in phenoxide ion, the charge is delocalised. The delocalisation of negative charge makes phenoxide ion more stable and favours the ionisation of phenol. In substituted phenols, the presence of electron withdrawing groups such as nitro group enhances the acidic strength of phenol. The stronger the acid, the lower the $pK_{a}$ value.
questions.explanation_html:
Key Idea Acidic strength is inversely proportional to the $pK_{a}$ value. The correct match is

$a \rightarrow iii,b \rightarrow iv,c \rightarrow i,d \rightarrow ii$

Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. The ionisation of an alcohol and a phenol takes place as follows

In alkoxide ion, the negative charge is localised on oxygen while in phenoxide ion, the charge is delocalised. The delocalisation of negative charge makes phenoxide ion more stable and favours the ionisation of phenol. In substituted phenols, the presence of electron withdrawing groups such as nitro group enhances the acidic strength of phenol. The stronger the acid, the lower the $pK_{a}$ value.
